NASA SWE-052 strongly supports the traceability and accountability portions of the design; W3C PROV-DM strongly supports a versioned provenance vocabulary for evidence, transformations, and responsible parties. Neither source mandates immutable snapshots, atomic decomposition, a particular evidence taxonomy, baselining workflow, or a “best” qualification architecture—those are reasonable design choices that must be stated as inferences and governed by project-specific rules.

## Official primary sources

- NASA Software Engineering Handbook, SWE-052 — Bidirectional Traceability Between Higher Level Requirements and Software Requirements:<https://swehb.nasa.gov/display/SWEHBVB/SWE-052+-+Bidirectional+Traceability+Between+Higher+Level+Requirements+and+Software+Requirements>Note: the page retrieved identifies itself as a handbook version associated with NPR 7150.2B; its central requirement text is: “The project manager shall perform, record, and maintain bidirectional traceability between the software requirement and the higher-level requirement.”
- W3C Recommendation, PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model, 30 April 2013:<https://www.w3.org/TR/2013/REC-prov-dm-20130430/>Current W3C report URL: <https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/>. PROV-DM is a conceptual, domain-agnostic provenance data model, not a requirements-engineering process standard.
- W3C Recommendation, PROV-CONSTRAINTS, 30 April 2013:<https://www.w3.org/TR/2013/REC-prov-constraints-20130430/>Current W3C report URL: <https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-constraints/>. It defines consistency/validity constraints for PROV records rather than proof that a requirement is satisfied.

## What the sources actually support


## NASA SWE-052

Supported facts
NASA’s guidance supports the following principles directly:
- Bidirectional links, recorded and maintained. SWE-052 requires the project manager to perform, record, and maintain bidirectional traceability between a software requirement and its higher-level requirement. NASA defines bidirectional traceability as an association discernible in both directions.
- Stable, unique requirement identification and source lineage. NASA recommends unique IDs that convey requirement hierarchy/lineage, capturing the requirement’s source, and including requirement text in the matrix rather than only an identifier.
- One canonical requirement record rather than copied requirement rows. NASA says to list a requirement once, show all its higher-level relationships with identifiers, and not duplicate requirements in the traceability matrix.
- Named maintenance accountability. NASA recommends assigning responsibility for creating and maintaining the matrix to a project team member, explicitly noting that link management is labor-intensive and needs tracking/monitoring.
- Forward and backward coverage through downstream artifacts. The guidance describes tracing requirements through design, implementation, and tests, and says bidirectional tracing can expose missing/incomplete functionality as well as code with no parent design element—extra functionality.
- Explicit gap handling. NASA says that orphan elements should be discussed by the project and assurance personnel. If necessary, missing source elements—such as requirements—are added. It also calls for justification when a requirement is not directly traceable to a higher-level requirement.
- Lifecycle review rather than a one-time matrix. NASA recommends creation early, maintenance throughout the project, sorting/reportability, and review at major phases or key reviews.
What SWE-052 does not establish
- It does not prescribe Git commits, hashes, immutable filesystems, signed attestations, content-addressed storage, or any other snapshot mechanism.
- It does not define “working,” “committed,” “installed,” “released,” or “live” evidence classes.
- It does not require each mixed-language requirement to be decomposed into mechanism/policy/provider atoms.
- It does not define semantic equivalence between a requirement and existing behavior.
- It does not say a baseline must be permanently frozen; instead, it says traceability must be maintained across the lifecycle. That matters for how “sealing” is framed.

## W3C PROV-DM

PROV-DM supports a model in which your requirements artifacts, evidence artifacts, qualification activities, and accountable actors can be explicitly represented:
- An entity is a physical, digital, conceptual, or other thing with fixed aspects. A particular source snapshot, a committed revision, a test report, an installation record, and an acceptance record can each be modeled as distinct entities.
- An activity occurs over time and uses, processes, modifies, or generates entities. Examples in PROV-DM include editing a file, publishing a document version, extracting metadata, and running a query.
- A derivation is a transformation, update, or construction of one entity from another. wasDerivedFrom can therefore describe a normalized criterion record derived from a source requirement, or an evidence report derived from a test execution—provided the claimed influence is real.
- PROV-DM distinguishes generation (wasGeneratedBy) and usage (used) from derivation. This is important: an activity may use an input and generate an output without the output necessarily being a derivation from every input used. PROV-DM explicitly says a usage-plus-generation chain is necessary but not sufficient for derivation; influence must also exist, and PROV deliberately does not define the domain conditions for deciding that.
- An agent bears some form of responsibility for an activity, an entity, or another agent’s activity. wasAssociatedWith assigns responsibility/role for an activity; wasAttributedTo ascribes an entity to an agent; actedOnBehalfOf expresses delegation with retained responsibility.
- A bundle is a named set of provenance descriptions and is itself an entity, enabling provenance of provenance. This is useful when the qualification record itself needs authorship, review, generation time, revision lineage, or an assessor.
- PROV supports different version/state descriptions of what may colloquially be called “the same thing.” Its constraints guidance explains that when relevant characteristics change, use multiple entities, each with an identifier, lifetime, and fixed attributes, and connect them through generation, usage, revision, invalidation, specialization, or alternate relationships as appropriate.
- PROV-CONSTRAINTS defines validity as consistent provenance history, with uniqueness, event ordering, typing, and impossibility constraints. It recommends that producers try to generate valid provenance.
What PROV-DM does not establish
- PROV validity is not evidence validity, test adequacy, security assurance, legal compliance, or proof of requirement satisfaction.
- wasDerivedFrom does not mean “semantically equivalent,” “correctly implements,” “meets,” “fully verifies,” or “is sufficient evidence for.”
- An agent association establishes a modeled responsibility relation; it does not establish competence, authorization, independence, or actual correctness of an assessment.
- The model does not determine how granular your entities, activities, or agents should be. It expressly leaves granularity choices to applications.
- It does not require immutability. “Fixed aspects” belongs to the conceptual identity of a PROV entity; project controls are still needed to make a stored artifact tamper-evident or practically immutable.
